“They know what a smart lad he is. He'll be a lifer. They'll give the Artful nothing less than life.”

“What do you mean by ‘lagging’ and ‘a lifer’?” demanded Mr. Bolter. “What's the use of talking like that to me? Why don't you say it so I can understand?”

Fagin was preparing to translate these obscure expressions into everyday language, which would have informed Mr. Bolter that they amounted to ‘transportation for life,’ when the arrival of Master Bates interrupted their conversation. His hands were buried in his trouser pockets, and his face was contorted into an expression of misery that bordered on the comical.

“It's all over, Fagin,” Charley said, once he and his new companion had been introduced.

“What do you mean?”

“They've located the gentleman the box belongs to; another two or three are coming to identify him, and the Artful's got his ticket overseas,” Master Bates answered. “I need a whole mourning outfit, Fagin, and a hatband, to pay him a visit before he goes on his travels. Imagine Jack Dawkins—splendid Jack—the Dodger—the Artful Dodger—being shipped abroad over a cheap little snuffbox! I never imagined he'd settle for anything less than a gold watch with its chain and seals. Why couldn't he have stolen every valuable some rich old gentleman possessed, and left the country like a gentleman himself, instead of a common thief without any honour or glory?”

After this expression of sympathy for his unlucky friend, Master Bates sank into the nearest chair, visibly frustrated and dejected.

“What do you mean, saying he's got no honour or glory?” Fagin exclaimed, glaring at his pupil. “Wasn't he always the best of you? Could a single one of you equal him, or even approach him, on any job? Eh?”

“Not one,” Master Bates replied, his voice hoarse with regret. “Not one.”

“Then why say it?” Fagin retorted angrily. “What are you blubbering about?”

“Because it won't be on the record, will it?” said Charley, whose mounting sorrow had driven him into open defiance of his venerable friend. “Because it can't go into the indictment; because nobody will ever know the half of what he was. What place will he have in the Newgate Calendar? Perhaps they won't mention him at all. Oh, hell, what a blow this is!”

“Ha, ha!” Fagin cried, extending his right hand and turning to Mr. Bolter. His chuckles shook his whole body as though he suffered from palsy. “Look at the pride they take in their profession, my dear.”

For a moment I was too astonished to think clearly. I knew my drawing differed greatly in detail from this one, although their general shapes were somewhat alike. Then I picked up a candle, sat at the far end of the room, and began examining the parchment more carefully. When I turned it over, I found my own sketch on the other side, exactly as I had drawn it. My first reaction was simply amazement at the remarkable resemblance between the outlines. What an extraordinary coincidence that, without my knowing it, a skull should have been drawn on the reverse of the parchment, directly behind my picture of the scarab, and that its size as well as its outline should so closely match my sketch! For a while, as I say, the strangeness of this coincidence left me utterly stunned. Such coincidences usually have that effect. The mind attempts to establish a connection, a chain of cause and effect; when it cannot, it falls into a kind of temporary paralysis. But as I emerged from that stupor, a conviction gradually formed that startled me much more than the coincidence itself. I began to remember distinctly, with absolute certainty, that there had been no picture on the parchment when I drew the scarab. I became completely sure of this, because I recalled turning it first one way and then the other to find the cleanest surface. If the skull had been there, I could not possibly have missed it. This was a mystery I felt unable to explain. Yet even at that early stage, somewhere in the furthest, most hidden recesses of my mind, a faint, glowworm-like idea seemed to shimmer: a hint of the truth that last night's adventure so magnificently confirmed. I stood up immediately, put the parchment safely away, and postponed any further thought until I could be alone.

“Once you had left and Jupiter was sound asleep, I began investigating the matter more systematically. First I considered how the parchment had come into my hands. We found the scarab on the mainland coast, about a mile east of the island and only a short way above the high-water mark. When I picked it up, it bit me sharply, making me drop it. Jupiter, cautious as always, looked around for a leaf or something similar before attempting to catch the insect, which had flown towards him. He wanted something he could use to take hold of it.”

“April 7th. Rose early, and to my extreme delight at last saw what I could unhesitatingly judge to be the northern Pole itself. There it unquestionably lay, directly below my feet; yet, alas, I had attained such an enormous height that no feature could be distinguished precisely. Indeed, from the successive figures recording my several elevations at various times between six A.M. on April the second and twenty minutes before nine that same morning, when the barometer ceased to register, one might reasonably conclude that by four o'clock this morning, April the seventh, the balloon had reached an altitude certainly no less than 7,254 miles above sea level. Vast as this elevation may seem, the reckoning upon which it rests probably yielded a figure considerably below the actual one. At any rate, I unquestionably saw the earth's entire major diameter. The whole northern hemisphere was spread beneath me like a map in orthographic projection, with the great equatorial circle itself marking the edge of my horizon. Your Excellencies will easily understand, however, that those restricted, still unexplored tracts within the Arctic circle, though lying immediately below me and therefore displayed without apparent foreshortening, were comparatively so small, and so remote from my point of observation, that no close scrutiny was possible. What I could discern was nevertheless strange and stirring. To the north of the immense ridge already described, which with a little qualification may be termed the boundary of human exploration in those parts, there stretches a single sheet of ice, uninterrupted or very nearly so. Over the first few degrees its surface becomes perceptibly flatter; farther on it sinks into a level plane; finally it grows markedly concave and ends at the Pole itself in a clearly outlined circular centre. The apparent diameter of this centre subtended an angle of some sixty-five seconds as viewed from the balloon. Its sombre colour varied in strength, but remained invariably darker than any other part of the hemisphere in sight, and sometimes deepened to an utterly impenetrable black. Beyond these particulars scarcely anything could be determined. By noon the circumference of the circular centre had notably diminished; by seven P.M. it had vanished from my view altogether, as the balloon crossed the western edge of the ice and drifted swiftly towards the equator.

“April 8th. Observed a perceptible reduction in the earth's apparent diameter, together with a considerable change in its overall colour and appearance.”
